data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["HTTP safety is about the *intent* of the method designer; log idempotency is about the *mechanism* of deduplication","HTTP idempotency is defined for the server's abstract resource state; log idempotency is about concrete byte-level log content","HTTP methods are a fixed enumeration; log operations are application-defined"],"overturn_conditions":["If RFC 9110 defines idempotency without requiring same-state convergence (e.g., only requiring 'no harmful' effects), the mathematical hierarchy breaks","If the log's deduplication mechanism is probabilistic rather than deterministic, idempotency is approximate rather than exact"],"shared_structure":["Safe: f(x) has no effect on state; Idempotent: f^n(x) = f(x) for all n >= 1","Safety is the stronger property: safe implies idempotent (vacuously, since no effect means repetition changes nothing)","Both are properties of operations under repetition"],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_005","SRC_006","SRC_008"],"transfer_claims":["The mathematical relationship (safe \u2282 idempotent) transfers from HTTP to any operation theory","The design pattern (use idempotency keys for at-least-once delivery) transfers from HTTP retry patterns to log append patterns"]},"claim":"RFC 9110 defines safe methods as those intended only for information retrieval with no side effects on server state, and idempotent methods as those where multiple identical requests have the same effect as a single request. The key distinction is that safety is about the *absence* of effects while idempotency is about the *convergence* of effects under repetition. An append-only event log requires idempotency of its writers \u2014 not safety \u2014 because appends produce state changes (entries in the log) but must be deduplicable so that at-least-once delivery does not create duplicate entries. Safety would paradoxically forbid the very operation (writing) that the log exists to perform.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the log's append operation is defined as 'create a new entry with a server-generated timestamp,' true idempotency is impossible because each retry produces a different timestamp.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the writer uses server-generated sequence numbers rather than client-generated identifiers, retries cannot be deduplicated and idempotency fails.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If RFC 9110's exact wording differs from the recalled definitions (e.g., using 'should not' vs 'must not' for safe methods), the precision of the distinction changes.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Per RFC 9110 \u00a79.2.1, safe methods are intended only for retrieval and should not have side effects. Per \u00a79.2.2, idempotent methods may have side effects but repeated identical requests must produce the same state as a single request. The append operation on a log is a side effect by definition \u2014 it adds data to the log. Therefore, append is not safe. But append can be made idempotent: if the writer assigns a stable unique identifier to each logical event, the log can detect and discard duplicate appends. Under at-least-once delivery, the network may deliver the same append request multiple times; idempotent appends ensure the log converges to the same state regardless of delivery count. This is the precise requirement: idempotency, not safety.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
